Baby & Child

Kyphosis in children: rounded backs, causes and care

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A rounded upper back can reflect flexible posture or a change in the shape of the spinal bones. These need different care. Many children have mild symptoms and do not need surgery, but a new or increasing curve deserves assessment. A child should not be blamed or repeatedly told to force the back straight before the cause is understood.

Normal spinal curves and excessive rounding

Viewed from the side, the spine has balancing curves: inward curves in the neck and lower back, and a gentle outward curve through the rib-bearing upper back. Vertebrae, discs, ligaments and muscles support it; the spinal canal protects the spinal cord. Kyphosis names the outward curve, while excessive rounding is often called hyperkyphosis. It is different from a side-to-side curve, although both may coexist.

The shape is often most noticeable in the thoracic upper back, but other regions can be involved. A clinician measures the curve on appropriate imaging and considers age, flexibility, growth and symptoms. Published angle definitions vary; a parent’s estimate, photograph or single numerical cutoff cannot diagnose the cause or decide whether treatment is needed.

Signs that merit an appointment

Rounded shoulders, a head held forward, uneven shoulder or shoulder-blade levels and a more prominent upper back when bending may be noticed. Tight hamstrings, back aching, stiffness or fatigue can occur. Some children have no pain. Arrange an appointment for a suspected curve, a changing shape, persistent discomfort or difficulty with everyday activities.

Severe curves can sometimes affect breathing, and structural curves may progress during growth or remain troublesome later. Rare neurological complications can affect walking, sensation or bladder function. Eating difficulty or reflux needs its own assessment rather than being automatically attributed to the spine. Pain, breathlessness or a new neurological symptom should not be dismissed as ordinary posture.

Causes and associated conditions

Sometimes no single cause is identified, and some structural forms occur in families. Congenital vertebral differences, Scheuermann disease, neuromuscular conditions such as cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy or spina bifida, and bone disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta may be involved. Injury, infection, a tumour or previous spinal treatment can also alter the spine. These are different mechanisms, not one diagnosis.

Metabolic or endocrine conditions may be considered when the medical history suggests them; a child with diabetes does not automatically have kyphosis or a predictable curve risk. Tell the clinician about development, family history, chronic illnesses, fractures, cancer treatment and previous surgery. Most rounded backs do not mean a tumour or serious neurological disease, but those possibilities are assessed when relevant.

Postural rounding and Scheuermann kyphosis

Postural rounding is flexible and the vertebrae have a normal shape. It can improve when the person changes position; symptoms are often limited. An examination distinguishes this from a fixed deformity. Supportive posture habits and suitable exercise can help comfort and function, without shaming a child or forcing a painful position.

Scheuermann kyphosis develops as the spine grows, often in adolescence. Several consecutive vertebrae become wedge-shaped, producing a more rigid curve that does not simply straighten on request. Pain may follow prolonged sitting, standing or activity, and the curve can involve the upper or lower thoracic region. Poor sitting posture alone does not explain these structural bone changes.

Congenital kyphosis needs an individual plan

In congenital kyphosis, one or more vertebrae did not form or separate normally before birth. The curve may be apparent early or become noticeable as the child grows. Different vertebral patterns progress differently; not every child has spinal-cord compression. Some also have other congenital conditions, so the specialist may assess more than the back.

A progressing sharp curve can threaten the spinal cord. Monitoring and treatment depend on the anatomy, growth and neurological findings, and surgery may be considered in a young child. Waiting until full height is not a universal rule. A paediatric spine team should explain the reason for the proposed timing and the benefits and risks of each option.

How the spine is assessed

Assessment includes symptoms, growth, medical and family history, examination of flexibility and alignment, and checks of strength, sensation and walking. Standing X-rays may measure the curve and show vertebral shape. MRI is selected for concerns such as neurological symptoms, congenital differences or rapid progression; CT or other tests are not automatically needed for every child.

The team balances useful information against radiation and other test burdens. Breathing tests or assessment of associated conditions may be appropriate. Ask what the diagnosis is, whether growth is likely to change it, which activities are suitable and when review is due. A planned review should be brought forward if the curve or symptoms change.

Observation, physiotherapy, bracing and surgery

A mild stable curve may need observation with visits during growth. Physiotherapy can address posture, strength, hamstring tightness, pain and function; it cannot promise to reshape rigid vertebrae or stop every structural curve progressing. Pain relief must suit the child’s age and health. A fitted brace may help selected growing children with Scheuermann kyphosis and needs specialist supervision and adjustment.

A brace is not a universal cure for severe or congenital deformity. Surgery may be considered for progressive congenital kyphosis or a severe, worsening or painful structural curve, especially with neurological or other major effects. Procedures can stabilize and partly correct the spine but carry risks, including infection, bleeding and nerve injury. Decisions and recovery are individual; neither a single angle nor reaching adult height determines every operation.

Prevention and day-to-day support

Not all childhood kyphosis can be prevented. Comfortable posture, appropriate activity and care for an underlying condition support health, but cannot prevent every congenital or developmental vertebral difference. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy reduces neural tube defects; that is not evidence that it prevents all congenital kyphosis. Parents should not be blamed for a child’s spinal shape.

Follow the team’s activity, brace and review plan, and ask for help with discomfort, school participation or body-image worries. Genetic advice may be useful for a relevant family history or associated syndrome, rather than being required for every child. Many children do well with appropriate follow-up, although long-term symptoms and treatment needs vary.

When to seek urgent or emergency help

Seek immediate emergency care for back pain with new weakness or numbness in both legs, loss of feeling around the genitals or anus, or new trouble passing urine or controlling bladder or bowel function. A serious accident with back pain also needs emergency assessment. Get emergency help for a child struggling to breathe, blue or grey lips or skin, or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for the next spine appointment or drive the child yourself when emergency transport is needed.

New walking difficulty, a neurological change, severe sudden or rapidly worsening back pain, or fever with back pain and feeling unwell need urgent same-day assessment; do not assume it is the known curve. Persistent night pain, unexplained weight loss, increasing deformity or breathing or swallowing difficulties also merit prompt medical review. Emergency features take priority over these routine review plans.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the clinician to distinguish a flexible postural curve from structural kyphosis and explain the child’s growth, imaging and follow-up plan. A photograph or angle estimate cannot replace assessment.

If a brace, exercise programme or surgery is suggested, ask what it can realistically achieve, how it will be monitored and what symptoms should trigger earlier review. Do not buy a corrective brace or force exercises without appropriate advice.

Seek urgent help for new neurological or walking symptoms, and use emergency care for the specific bladder/bowel, bilateral-leg, injury or breathing warnings. Do not attribute every new symptom to an existing spine diagnosis.

How BeMama can help

A rounded back is not proof of poor parenting, a particular disease or a need for surgery. The useful distinction is the child’s specific flexible or structural pattern, how it changes with growth and how it affects comfort and function.

When to seek help

Get immediate emergency care for back pain with new weakness or numbness in both legs, loss of feeling around the genitals or anus, or new urinary or bowel-control difficulty, and after a serious accident. A child struggling to breathe, turning blue or grey or becoming less responsive also needs emergency help. New walking or other neurological changes, fever with back pain and illness, or severe sudden or rapidly worsening back pain need urgent same-day assessment; do not wait for a scheduled review.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Flexible postural rounding and structural vertebral changes need different care.
  • A suspected or increasing childhood curve deserves assessment even without pain.
  • Growth, symptoms and the type of curve guide monitoring, bracing and surgery.
  • Exercises and braces cannot promise to correct every structural deformity.
  • New neurological, bladder/bowel or major breathing symptoms must not wait for a routine appointment.

Frequently asked questions

What can cause a child’s rounded back?

Flexible posture, congenital vertebral differences, Scheuermann disease and some bone or neuromuscular conditions are possibilities. Injury, infection, tumours or earlier spinal treatment can also contribute. Appearance alone cannot identify the cause.

What does congenital kyphosis mean?

It means vertebrae did not form or separate normally before birth. The curve may become clearer during growth. Progression and spinal-cord risk vary, so paediatric specialist monitoring and sometimes early treatment are needed.

What complications can occur?

Many children have mild symptoms. Some develop pain or a worsening curve; severe deformity can affect breathing and occasionally neurological function. New walking, sensation or bladder/bowel changes need medical assessment, with emergency care for the warning signs described above.

Can all kyphosis be prevented with posture or folic acid?

No. Healthy posture and activity can support comfort, but do not prevent all structural changes. Folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects; it has not been shown to prevent every congenital kyphosis. The child or parent should not be blamed.

Can exercises straighten a structural curve?

Physiotherapy may improve strength, flexibility, pain and function. It does not guarantee that rigid wedge-shaped vertebrae will change or that progression will stop. Use an individual plan rather than forcing painful stretches.

Does every child need a brace or surgery?

No. Some need observation only. Bracing is an option for selected growing children, especially with Scheuermann kyphosis. Surgery depends on the type, progression, symptoms and risks; congenital cases may need earlier intervention rather than waiting until growth ends.

Does every child need MRI or CT?

No. Examination and suitable X-rays often provide key information. MRI, CT, breathing tests or other investigations are selected for specific concerns, balancing benefits and burdens. Ask why each test is proposed.

Which symptoms need emergency care?

Back pain with new symptoms in both legs, loss of feeling around the genitals or anus, or new bladder/bowel difficulty needs emergency assessment. So do back pain after a serious accident, major breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a routine spine visit.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
